input_signals.name: Externally financed asset growth
input_signals.hypothesis: Asset growth is only value-destroying when the firm cannot fund it from internal cash flow; expansion by free-cash-flow-negative (low-quality) firms reflects empire building and external capital dependence, whereas self-funded growth is disciplined.
input_signals.reasoning: The indicator switches asset growth on only for firms whose operating cash flow fails to cover capex, isolating the fragile-expansion subset from the productive-expansion subset. Internally funded growers keep a zero signal and are pooled at the neutral point, so the long-short spread is driven by financing-constrained overinvestors rather than by the unconditional asset-growth effect. Coverage stays broad because oancf, capx and at are widely reported.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( growth( at, 1 ), indicator( neg( ratio( sub( oancf, capx ), at ) ), 0 ) )

input_signals.name: Inventory bloat with weak profitability
input_signals.hypothesis: Working-capital investment that outruns sales growth indicates demand misjudgment; this is far more informative about future returns at low-profitability firms, which lack the margin cushion to absorb obsolete or discounted inventory.
input_signals.reasoning: The first term is an investment-quality wedge (inventory growth in excess of sales growth), and the rank of negative three-year average ROA weights it toward structurally weak firms. High-ROA firms building inventory ahead of demand are treated as near-neutral, so the spread reflects unproductive working-capital expansion instead of generic asset growth.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( growth( invt, 1 ), growth( sale, 1 ) ), rank( neg( ma( ratio( ib, at ), 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Financing-deficit-weighted capacity growth
input_signals.hypothesis: Growth in gross physical capacity destroys value when the firm's investment outlay exceeds internally generated operating cash flow, and is benign or value-creating when capacity is added out of internal cash; the same expansion therefore carries opposite information depending on internal funding capacity.
input_signals.reasoning: This repairs the gen-0 zero-mass failure: the binary FCF-negative switch is replaced by a continuous, industry-demeaned financing-deficit z-score, so every firm receives a signed weight and the quantile breakpoints are non-degenerate while the strong cross-sectional slope channel is preserved. Self-funded capacity builders now load on the long leg rather than piling up at exactly zero, which should convert the gen-0 FMB t-stat of -3.9 into a real long-short alpha.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( ppegt, 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( capx, oancf ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Expansion beyond replacement at low cash profitability
input_signals.hypothesis: Capex far in excess of depreciation is net capacity expansion rather than maintenance; expansion is only justified when the existing asset base already generates high cash profitability, so aggressive net expansion by cash-poor firms signals overinvestment.
input_signals.reasoning: Scaling capex by depreciation separates replacement investment from genuine expansion using the firm's own capital-consumption benchmark, a distinct construction from asset or capex growth rates, and the signed industry-demeaned three-year cash-ROA multiplier flips the interpretation across quality tiers instead of merely attenuating it. Both legs are continuous and densely populated, so portfolio composition should be stable.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( capx, dp ) ), neg( ind_zscore( ma( ratio( oancf, at ), 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Equity-funded growth without retained earnings
input_signals.hypothesis: Financing expansion with new equity is most damaging at firms with little or negative accumulated retained earnings, because such firms have no demonstrated history of internally generating profit and are effectively funding unproven growth with market capital.
input_signals.reasoning: Retained earnings scaled by assets is a stock measure of cumulative earnings quality and firm maturity, a different quality dimension from flow profitability, accruals, or volatility used elsewhere in the archive. Interacting it with equity-issuance intensity separates seasoned self-financed issuers (long leg) from cash-burning issuers (short leg), and both inputs are broadly reported so coverage should match the archive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sstk, at ) ), neg( ind_zscore( ratio( re, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity growth minus gross-profit growth
input_signals.hypothesis: Productive investment shows up as gross profit growing at least as fast as the physical asset base it is built on; when capacity and inventory expand faster than gross profit, the new assets are not earning, signaling low-quality expansion and future disappointment.
input_signals.reasoning: This generalizes the one gen-0 winner from inventory-versus-sales to total physical capacity versus gross profit, making the quality benchmark a margin-bearing flow rather than raw revenue, and it embeds the interaction in the wedge itself rather than as a multiplicative weight — which the critic noted only attenuates. It is a self-scaling, densely populated signal that avoids both zero-mass and rank-attenuation failure modes.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( sub( growth( add( ppegt, invt ), 1 ), growth( sub( revt, cogs ), 1 ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Investment-quality rank divergence
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters is whether a firm's capital expansion is commensurate with its demonstrated operating quality and balance-sheet capacity: firms whose investment rank far exceeds their quality rank are over-extending, while firms whose quality exceeds their investment rank retain unexploited internal capacity.
input_signals.reasoning: Both channels are industry-ranked on the same bounded scale and enter with equal weight and opposite signs, so the signal cannot be an attenuated quality composite — its dispersion comes from the mismatch between the two themes rather than from the quality score alone. Replacing five-year earnings volatility with cash profitability and leverage keeps the quality gauge economically rich while preserving coverage, and the difference-of-ranks structure is a genuinely different design from the multiplicative and wedge families already in the archive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( ind_rank( winsor( growth( ppent, 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( sumrank( ma( ratio( oancf, at ), 3 ), neg( ratio( lt, at ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Investing into falling capital productivity
input_signals.hypothesis: Adding capacity while the existing asset base is generating progressively less revenue per dollar of assets signals overcapacity and demand misjudgment, whereas heavy investment accompanied by rising asset turnover reflects capacity that is already being absorbed.
input_signals.reasoning: The quality gauge is capital productivity change rather than a profitability or accrual level, so the signal is not another q-theory profitability interaction, and the denominators (ppent for investment intensity, at for turnover) avoid the mechanical small-PPE artifact that a sale/ppe pairing would create. Utilization deterioration is observable before margins deteriorate, so it may lead the profitability-based versions in the archive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( capx, ppent ), 1 ) ), neg( ind_zscore( winsor( delta( ratio( sale, at ), 1 ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cash-buffer depletion during expansion
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(DELTA(RATIO(che, at), 1), MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Heavy investment financed by drawing down liquid reserves at firms that also generate weak operating cash flow is the most fragile form of expansion, since both the internal flow and the stock of internal funding are being exhausted simultaneously.
input_signals.reasoning: This separates the stock (change in cash holdings) from the flow (three-year cash ROA) dimension of internal funding and co-ranks them, rather than using the capx-minus-oancf gap, so it is not a rescaling of the archive's winner but a test of whether the liquidity buffer carries independent information. Both inputs are densely reported, so coverage should exceed the archive's funding-gap signals.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( capx, at ), 1 ) ), neg( ind_zscore( sumrank( delta( ratio( che, at ), 1 ), ma( ratio( oancf, at ), 3 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity added beyond internal funding capacity
input_signals.hypothesis: The economically meaningful quantity is how far a firm's capacity additions exceed the cash its operations actually produced: large positive gaps are externally funded expansion, while large negative values are cash-generative firms holding capacity flat or shrinking, which should be rewarded.
input_signals.reasoning: Retaining the deficit magnitude on a common asset scale fixes the quadrant problem in the SIGN version: cash-rich firms that shrink now receive the most negative (bullish) values, consistent with both the asset-growth and profitability evidence, instead of being predicted to underperform. The construct is a single dense continuous variable with no rank attenuation, no zero mass, and both themes entering symmetrically, so a strong result is direct evidence that the investment-versus-internal-cash gap, not either level alone, is the priced quantity.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( delta( ppegt, 1 ), oancf ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Capex intensity with weak debt-service capacity
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), ADD(dltt, dlc)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Capital spending is dangerous when cash earnings cover only a small fraction of outstanding debt, because the firm must keep servicing fixed claims while the new assets are still unproductive, forcing asset sales or dilution exactly when the investment fails to pay off.
input_signals.reasoning: Debt-service capacity (funds from operations over total debt) is a distinct fragility dimension from the flow funding gap, the cash buffer, or working-capital slack already tested, and it directly captures the claim-priority mechanism behind low-quality expansion. Funds from operations and debt balances are densely reported, so coverage should be at the higher end of the archive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( capx, at ), 1 ) ), neg( ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( add( ib, dp ), add( dltt, dlc ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capex into a multi-year gross-profitability decline
input_signals.hypothesis: Adding capacity while gross profitability on the asset base has been declining for several years signals structural erosion of the business rather than a temporary dip, and such investment should be punished more than investment during a one-year turnover wobble.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's capital-productivity signal produced a solid FMB slope but almost no alpha, consistent with a noisy one-year change in asset turnover producing unstable portfolio extremes; replacing it with a five-year trend in gross profit over assets smooths the quality leg and shifts the concept from utilization wobble to structural erosion. This isolates the smoothing/horizon choice while keeping the same capital-productivity mechanism.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( capx, ppent ), 1 ) ), neg( ind_zscore( winsor( trend( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), at ), 5 ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Aging capital base with weak cash generation
input_signals.hypothesis: A heavily depreciated capital stock means the productive base is old and due for replacement; firms in that state with weak cash generation cannot fund renewal and face obsolescence, whereas cash-rich firms with old assets can harvest or reinvest at will.
input_signals.reasoning: Capital vintage — accumulated depreciation as a share of gross property — is an investment-theme state variable measuring past *under*-investment, the opposite pole from every expansion measure in the archive, so this tests whether the theme interaction is symmetric or specific to overexpansion. Pairing it with three-year cash ROA distinguishes obsolescence traps (short leg) from mature cash-generative harvesters (long leg), and both inputs are densely reported.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( sub( ppegt, ppent ), ppegt ), 1 ) ), neg( ind_zscore( ma( ratio( oancf, at ), 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Expansion financed through losses
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(ib, at), ABS(RATIO(ib, at))), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Quality matters asymmetrically for investment: variation in profitability among already-profitable firms says little about whether capex is productive, but the depth of current losses says a great deal, because loss-making expanders must fund both operations and growth from outside capital.
input_signals.reasoning: The term ib/at minus its absolute value equals twice the loss magnitude and is exactly zero for every profitable firm, so the quality leg conditions only within the loss region instead of spreading weight across the whole profitability distribution — an asymmetric conditioning design the archive has never tested. The short leg is deep-loss heavy investors, the long leg is profitable heavy investors, which is precisely the productive-versus-fragile expansion contrast the theme asks for.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( capx, at ), 1 ) ), neg( ind_zscore( winsor( sub( ratio( ib, at ), abs( ratio( ib, at ) ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity growth with chronic deficit years
input_signals.hypothesis: What distinguishes structurally external-finance-dependent expanders from firms in a lumpy capex year is the *number* of past years in which investment exceeded operating cash flow; capacity growth by firms with a persistent deficit history should be the most value-destroying.
input_signals.reasoning: Counting deficit years over five years converts the funding-gap concept from a heavy-tailed magnitude into a bounded 0–5 state variable, so it cannot be dominated by outliers and it measures persistence rather than the current-year level — a different economic claim (chronic dependence) from the archive's one-year gap. If it beats the one-year winner on the FMB slope while holding the alpha, it identifies persistence as the operative fragility mechanism.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( growth( ppegt, 1 ) ), ind_zscore( ts_sum( indicator( ratio( sub( capx, oancf ), at ), 0 ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capex with near-term refinancing pressure
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dlc, ADD(ib, dp)), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms committing cash to long-lived assets while their debt maturing within the year exceeds a full year of cash earnings face rollover risk exactly during the project gestation period, forcing distressed refinancing, asset sales, or dilution.
input_signals.reasoning: This repairs the failed maturity-mismatch signal, whose lct/lt leg inadvertently proxied for *low* leverage (giving the wrong sign); the replacement measures near-term debt net of annual funds from operations on a common asset scale, so loss-making firms with maturing debt score most fragile instead of being mis-ranked by a negative denominator. It is distinct from the FFO-to-total-debt signal because it isolates *timing* of claims rather than total leverage capacity.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( capx, at ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( dlc, add( ib, dp ) ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Inventory bloat with signed cash profitability
input_signals.hypothesis: Working-capital investment outrunning sales is bearish at cash-poor firms and largely innocuous at cash-generative firms, which can carry and eventually clear the inventory; the quality leg should therefore reorder the wedge rather than merely shrink it.
input_signals.reasoning: The gen-0 inventory-bloat winner used a non-negative ROA rank that could only attenuate, which the critic identified as its central weakness; replacing it with a signed, industry-standardized three-year cash-ROA and ranking the wedge itself makes high-bloat cash-poor firms the short leg and high-bloat cash-rich firms the long leg. This is an attributable single-element upgrade of an established archive winner along the dimension the critic flagged.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( sub( growth( invt, 1 ), growth( sale, 1 ) ), 1 ) ), neg( ind_zscore( ma( ratio( oancf, at ), 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Expansion on receivable-inflated revenue
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(GROWTH(SUB(SUB(act, invt), che), 1), GROWTH(sale, 1)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Capital spending justified by revenue that is being generated through looser credit terms rather than cash sales is built on a demand signal that will not persist; firms expanding capacity while receivables grow faster than sales are extrapolating low-quality revenue.
input_signals.reasoning: The quality dimension here is *revenue* quality — the receivable-versus-sales growth wedge, using non-cash non-inventory current assets — which is economically distinct from every quality leg tested so far (cash-flow funding gap, solvency slack, profitability level, accruals, leverage) and is the channel through which managers most often misread demand before committing capital. It abandons the over-explored solvency-slack interaction entirely while keeping the multiplicative conditioning structure that has generated the archive's alphas, and all inputs are densely reported one-year flows.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( capx, at ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( sub( growth( sub( sub( act, invt ), che ), 1 ), growth( sale, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity growth on receivable-inflated revenue
input_signals.hypothesis: Building capacity in response to revenue growth that is being manufactured through looser customer credit rather than cash sales is expansion premised on a demand signal that will reverse.
input_signals.reasoning: The revenue-quality wedge (receivables growing faster than sales) delivered the strongest FMB slope of the gen-4 batch (−2.97) but only −0.9% alpha when attached to capex intensity; pairing it with capacity growth tests the same investment-leg diagnosis on an entirely different quality channel, so the two swaps jointly identify whether the carrier or the channel governs portfolio performance. Both legs are one-year flows, keeping coverage near the archive's high end.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( growth( ppegt, 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( sub( growth( sub( sub( act, invt ), che ), 1 ), growth( sale, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity growth co-ranked with loss depth
input_signals.hypothesis: Fragile expansion is the joint occurrence of growing productive capacity and running losses; both features should push the signal in the same bearish direction, so that shrinking profitable firms occupy the long leg and expanding loss-makers the short leg.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic correctly showed that z-scoring then negating the hinge gave profitable firms a common negative multiplier, making the long leg high-growth profitable firms — a bet against the asset-growth effect that the hypothesis never intended. Co-ranking instead keeps the loss channel non-negative (|x|−x equals twice the loss magnitude, zero for profitable firms) and lets capacity growth enter monotonically bearish on its own, so no quadrant contradicts either the investment or the quality evidence while the interaction still concentrates the short leg on expanding loss-makers.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( winsor( growth( ppegt, 1 ), 1 ), neg( sub( ratio( ib, at ), abs( ratio( ib, at ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Multi-channel expansion breadth with internal funding gap
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(ADD(ADD(INDICATOR(GROWTH(ppegt, 1), 0), INDICATOR(GROWTH(invt, 1), 0)), INDICATOR(RATIO(COALESCE(aqc, 0), at), 0))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(capx, oancf), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms expanding on every front at once — physical capacity, inventory, and acquisitions simultaneously — are in an empire-building mode that is far more dangerous when internal cash does not cover the investment programme than any single expansion channel is on its own.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than tweaking the winner's deficit numerator, this changes the carrier's structure entirely: breadth is a 0–3 count of simultaneously expanding investment channels, a diversification-of-growth-modes concept that no archive signal captures and that cannot be reproduced by any single growth rate. Pairing the new carrier with the unmodified, proven funding-gap quality leg keeps the comparison to the archive's best signal clean and attributable to the breadth construction alone.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( add( add( indicator( growth( ppegt, 1 ), 0 ), indicator( growth( invt, 1 ), 0 ) ), indicator( ratio( coalesce( aqc, 0 ), at ), 0 ) ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( capx, oancf ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Profitable expanders with an internal funding gap
input_signals.expression: MUL(MUL(RANK(GROWTH(ppegt, 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(capx, oancf), at), 1))), IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The overinvestment penalty applies to viable firms that expand beyond their internal cash generation; deep-loss expanders are a separate distress population whose returns are driven by option-like recovery risk, so weighting the funding-gap interaction toward profitable firms should sharpen the abnormal-return spread.
input_signals.reasoning: The gen-5 loss-depth result showed that the deep-loss expansion tail earns strongly *positive* FF5 alpha, which means any signal that pushes loss-makers into the short leg is fighting a distress premium; multiplying the archive's best interaction by a non-negative profitability rank smoothly pulls loss-makers toward the middle without creating a zero mass. The long leg becomes profitable, self-funded expanders and the short leg profitable but externally dependent expanders — precisely the productive-versus-unproductive contrast, purged of distress.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( mul( rank( growth( ppegt, 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( capx, oancf ), at ), 1 ) ) ), ind_rank( ratio( ib, at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity growth with flow and stock funding fragility
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(ppegt, 1)), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(capx, oancf), at), NEG(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), lt)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Fragile expansion has two complementary funding dimensions — a flow shortfall (investment exceeding operating cash flow) and a stock shortfall (little working-capital slack against liabilities) — and firms failing both are the most exposed when new capacity disappoints.
input_signals.reasoning: These are the only two quality channels in the archive that have produced FF5 alphas beyond 3% annualized, and their weaknesses are complementary: the flow gap delivers the cross-sectional slope, the stock slack delivers the largest alphas but no slope. Co-ranking them inside the quality leg (bounded, so neither dominates through outliers) while holding the growth carrier fixed is a single attributable change aimed at getting slope and alpha from one construct.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( ppegt, 1 ) ), ind_zscore( sumrank( ratio( sub( capx, oancf ), at ), neg( ratio( sub( act, lct ), lt ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity growth funded by outside equity
input_signals.hypothesis: The portion of a firm's book-equity increase not explained by its own earnings is external equity finance net of distributions; capacity growth paid for with outside equity rather than retained profit signals expansion the market must fund rather than expansion the business has earned.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the failed gross-issuance measure (sstk, which is contaminated by option exercises and produced almost no alpha) with a clean net measure — the change in book equity less current earnings — which nets dividends and buybacks and is defined for essentially every firm. It tests a funding *source* channel distinct from cash-flow shortfall, since a firm can have a small operating gap yet still be systematically diluting shareholders to grow.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( growth( ppegt, 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( delta( ceq, 1 ), ib ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity growth against the binding funding constraint
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(ppegt, 1)), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, capx), at)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), lt))))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Financial fragility is set by a firm's weakest funding dimension rather than by an average of its dimensions: a firm with ample cash flow but no balance-sheet slack, or ample slack but a large cash shortfall, is exposed either way, so expansion should be punished according to the binding constraint.
input_signals.reasoning: Taking the minimum of the two ranked funding channels is a conjunctive, weakest-link aggregation that no archive signal uses, and it is a substantively different economic claim from the co-ranked average version — one says fragility compounds, the other says the binding constraint governs — so the pair jointly identifies how fragility aggregates rather than re-testing additive versus multiplicative structure. Ranking each channel before the MIN keeps the two dimensions on a common scale so neither can dominate through units or outliers.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( ppegt, 1 ) ), neg( ind_zscore( min( ind_rank( ratio( sub( oancf, capx ), at ) ), ind_rank( ratio( sub( act, lct ), lt ) ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity growth with weak internal coverage of capex
input_signals.hypothesis: The economically meaningful quantity is what fraction of the investment programme operations actually pay for; a firm spending twice its operating cash flow is externally dependent regardless of how large that gap looks relative to total assets.
input_signals.reasoning: Normalizing internal cash by the investment programme rather than by the asset base removes the capital-intensity and size contamination in the (capx − oancf)/at scaling, and ranking the coverage ratio before standardizing handles the sign and scale pathologies that arise when operating cash flow is negative. This is a different economic normalization of the winning channel, not a rescaling of the same variable, so a comparison directly tests which funding metric the market prices.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( ppegt, 1 ) ), neg( ind_zscore( ind_rank( ratio( oancf, capx ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Multi-year net capital formation against funding shortfall
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(capx, dp), 3), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(capx, oancf), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Genuine expansion is capital spending in excess of capital consumption sustained over several years; firms that have been adding net capital for three years while still failing to fund investment internally are the clearest cases of persistent, externally financed overexpansion.
input_signals.reasoning: The carrier becomes cumulative *net* capital formation (capex less depreciation over three years, asset-scaled), which strips replacement investment and single-year lumpiness from the expansion measure — a different investment state variable than either a one-year growth rate or a gross cumulative capex total. Holding the funding-gap leg unchanged keeps the comparison to the leading signal clean and tests whether persistence of net capital formation, rather than the current year's expansion, is the operative investment condition.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( winsor( ratio( ts_sum( sub( capx, dp ), 3 ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( capx, oancf ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Hiring commitments against internal funding shortfall
input_signals.hypothesis: Headcount growth is the least reversible investment a firm makes — wages must be paid every period and layoffs are costly — so hiring while investment already exceeds internal cash generation commits the firm to a fixed cash burden it cannot fund, whereas cash-generative firms can carry new staff through a slow patch.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the coverage patch with a substantively different investment channel: the carrier is an off-balance-sheet, irreversible labor commitment rather than capitalized property, which tests whether the funding-fragility mechanism is about capital formation specifically or about committing to any fixed obligation without internal funds. Employment is reported far more broadly and uniformly than gross PP&E, so tradable breadth improves for an economic reason rather than through a missing-data substitution.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( growth( emp, 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( capx, oancf ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity growth during an inventory glut
input_signals.hypothesis: Inventory sitting at a multi-year high relative to sales means the firm cannot clear what it already produces; adding productive capacity in that state compounds an existing glut, while expanding when stock is lean relative to sales indicates demand genuinely pulling product through.
input_signals.reasoning: The quality gauge is the firm's own inventory-to-sales *position in its five-year history* — a demand-absorption state rather than the one-year inventory-versus-sales growth wedge or a margin change, so it is not a repackaging of the margin-deterioration channel the critic identified. It is bounded, firm-normalized, and densely available, and it pairs a working-capital state with the physical-capacity carrier that has produced the archive's largest alphas.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( growth( ppegt, 1 ) ), ind_zscore( ts_rank( ratio( invt, sale ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity growth with funding gap and inventory glut
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(ppegt, 1)), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(capx, oancf), at), TS_RANK(RATIO(invt, sale), 5))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Expansion is worst when the firm can neither fund it internally nor sell what it already produces; the cash-shortfall and demand-absorption conditions are economically distinct and should reinforce each other.
input_signals.reasoning: The glut conditioner produced the archive's strongest Fama-MacBeth slope (−4.39) with a weak alpha, while the funding gap produces the strongest alphas with a moderate slope, so their weaknesses are complementary in exactly the way the flow-plus-stock merge was — and that merge held its alpha at −4.1% with t −3.46. Both channels are bounded before co-ranking (the glut term is a firm-normalized five-year position, the gap winsorized), so neither can dominate through outliers.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( ppegt, 1 ) ), ind_zscore( sumrank( ratio( sub( capx, oancf ), at ), ts_rank( ratio( invt, sale ), 5 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Inventory investment against the funding gap
input_signals.hypothesis: Working-capital investment is a resource commitment like capital and labor; building stock while investment already exceeds operating cash flow means the firm is financing unsold goods with outside money.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the third and final distinct commitment channel — after fixed capital and labor — and tests whether the funding-fragility mechanism is general to all resource commitments or specific to long-lived assets, which is the key question for interpreting the whole archive. Inventory change scaled by lagged assets is dense and free of the small-denominator problem in growth-rate carriers.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( delta( invt, 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( capx, oancf ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Out-of-character expansion against the funding gap
input_signals.hypothesis: What signals over-extrapolation is not being a high-investment firm but making an unusually large commitment relative to the firm's own recent behaviour; a capacity jump to the top of a firm's own five-year expansion range, undertaken without internal cash, is a discretionary bet rather than a steady capital programme.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the averaging of two known parents with a genuine economic distinction the archive has never separated — cross-sectionally high expansion (partly an industry characteristic) versus expansion that is unusual for the firm — using the firm's own history to define the commitment. Habitual capital-intensive firms are pushed toward the middle regardless of their level of capex, so the extreme portfolios consist of firms changing behaviour, which is where extrapolation errors should concentrate.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ts_rank( growth( ppegt, 1 ), 5 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( capx, oancf ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Inventory building into an existing overhang
input_signals.hypothesis: Adding stock when inventory relative to sales already stands at the top of the firm's own five-year range is unambiguous evidence of unsold production, whereas building stock from a lean base reflects demand the firm expects to fill.
input_signals.reasoning: This pairs the working-capital commitment channel with the demand-absorption state that matches it economically, rather than borrowing the physical-capacity carrier as the earlier glut test did, so the interaction is internally coherent: both legs describe inventory. Its inputs are dense and it needs neither cash-flow statement nor five-year capital history, so it complements the funding-gap family with an independent, high-coverage mechanism.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( delta( invt, 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( ts_rank( ratio( invt, sale ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity growth with confirmed uses and sources shortfall
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(ppegt, 1)), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(capx, oancf), at), RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), ib)), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm is genuinely externally dependent only when both sides of its funding identity agree — investment exceeds internal cash *and* the firm actually went to capital markets to close the difference — so requiring both should purge measurement noise from either leg alone.
input_signals.reasoning: The uses-side gap has produced the archive's best alpha and the sources-side issuance measure its second-best slope, and unlike previous merges (gap with solvency slack, gap with inventory glut) these two legs measure the *same* economic event through independent accounting channels, so co-ranking them is a noise-reduction argument rather than an aggregation of different risks. If the combination lifts the alpha t-statistic above the leader's −3.95, it would be the strongest construct discovered in this search.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( ppegt, 1 ) ), ind_zscore( sumrank( ratio( sub( capx, oancf ), at ), ratio( add( delta( add( dltt, dlc ), 1 ), sub( delta( ceq, 1 ), ib ) ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity growth with weak debt-service capacity
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm whose annual cash earnings cover only a small fraction of its outstanding debt has no capacity to absorb a disappointing project; expanding capacity from that position means the fixed claims must be serviced throughout the gestation of assets that may never earn.
input_signals.reasoning: Debt-service capacity is a *stock* leverage-capacity condition, economically distinct from the flow funding gap and from the net-external-financing quantity the critic identified as published, and it is the one quality channel in the archive that produced a genuine alpha (−2.2%, t −2.41) while attached to the capex-*level* carrier that the archive has repeatedly shown suppresses alpha. Re-pairing it with the validated capacity-growth carrier is the single highest-prior untested combination remaining, and its inputs support coverage near 0.118 rather than the leader's 0.076.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( ppegt, 1 ) ), neg( ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( add( ib, dp ), add( dltt, dlc ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Persistent net expansion without internal funding
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(TS_SUM(MUL(INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(capx, dp), at), 0), INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(capx, oancf), at), 0)), 3)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(capx, oancf), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Undisciplined capital allocation is a repeated pattern: adding capital beyond replacement needs while failing to fund it internally, in year after year, identifies management behaviour rather than a single lumpy project.
input_signals.reasoning: The degeneracy the critic identified is removed by replacing the near-always-true "gross PP&E rose" test with "capex exceeded depreciation," a genuinely binding condition satisfied by roughly half of firm-years, so the three-year count now measures the joint state rather than collapsing to a deficit count. Severity is retained through the current-year gap magnitude, giving a construct that separates chronic over-expanders from firms whose shortfall is a one-off, which the archive's earlier persistence tests could not do.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ts_sum( mul( indicator( ratio( sub( capx, dp ), at ), 0 ), indicator( ratio( sub( capx, oancf ), at ), 0 ) ), 3 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( capx, oancf ), at ), 1 ) ) )
